Solving the expansion for the estimation error ˆ︁ δδ gives its linearization, a linear function of the estimating functions g(δ; γ 𝑖 ), namely their sum multiplied by -A(δ) -1 , so the inverse bread matrix A -1 translates the variability of the estimating functions into that of ˆ︁ δ, and a linking method whose estimating functions react only weakly to δ turns the same variability of the estimating functions into a larger LE.

The variance of the linearization (Eq. 6) is the sandwich variance, which approximates the variance of ˆ︁ δ with an accuracy that increases with the number of items 𝐼 (Boos & Stefanski, 2013; Stefanski & Boos, 2002),

The sandwich variance refers to the parameter that the estimating equations define, which under misspecification is a pseudo-true parameter in the sense of White (1982) (Berk et al., 2014; Stefanski & Boos, 2002). The sandwich variance therefore does not require the item response model to hold, which matters in LSAs, whose scaling models are approximations rather than datagenerating mechanisms (cf. Longford, 2012). For the same reason, the LE and SE estimators of the following subsections do not depend on the zero-mean assumption (Robitzsch, 2023; Stefanski & Boos, 2002), and without zero means, the closed forms derived below hold with the pseudo-true parameters and the IPD effects centered at their means. Summing the covariance matrices in the meat matrix B item by item presupposes that the IPD effects are uncorrelated across items. This is an assumption on the IPD process, the model that generates the IPD effects, such as the random walk (Eq. 3), and not on the item responses. The item responses remain dependent, because the same persons respond to all items of a time point (Boos & Stefanski, 2013).

With infinite person samples, the calibrated item parameters γ 𝑖 carry no sampling error, so the variability of the estimating functions stems from the IPD effects alone. For item 𝑖, the IPD effects are collected in the IPD vector o 𝑖 = ( 𝑓 𝑖2 , . . . , 𝑓 𝑖𝑇 , 𝑒 𝑖2 , . . . , 𝑒 𝑖𝑇 ) ⊤ with the within-item covariance matrix 𝚽, whose diagonal contains the IPD variances τ² 𝑓 𝑡 and τ² 𝑒 𝑡 . The off-diagonal entries of 𝚽 contain the covariances of the IPD effects. Each IPD effect carries the index of the time point it leads to, so the subscript 𝑡 also indexes the link from 𝑡 -1 to 𝑡. The covariance between the discrimination and the difficulty IPD effect of the same link, that is, of the same LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS two consecutive time points, such as τ 𝑓 𝑡 𝑒 𝑡 , is a within-link covariance. The covariance between IPD effects of different links, such as τ 𝑒 𝑡 𝑒 𝑡 ′ or τ 𝑓 𝑡 𝑒 𝑡 ′ with 𝑡 ≠ 𝑡 ′ , is a cross-link covariance. No restriction is imposed on 𝚽 at this point. If the estimating function is linear in the IPD vector, g(δ; γ 𝑖 ) = L 𝑖 o 𝑖 for a matrix L 𝑖 that depends on the linking method and on the administration pattern d 𝑖 of item 𝑖, inserting L 𝑖 o 𝑖 into the meat matrix B of Equation ( 5)gives which separates the IPD process in 𝚽 from the linking method in L 𝑖 .

A target quantity, such as a linked mean or a linked SD, is a scalar function ℎ(δ) of the entries of δ, in general a nonlinear one. A linked SD is the exponential of a log SD, and if δ contains the parameters of each link, a linked parameter of a later time point combines the entries of several links. The LE of a target quantity follows from the delta method with the vector u of the partial derivatives of ℎ (Boos & Stefanski, 2013),

Linking Error Estimators

Evaluating the bread matrix A and the meat matrix B at the true parameter vector δ, with the true IPD variances and covariances in the within-item covariance matrix 𝚽, gives the expected sandwich variance (Boos & Stefanski, 2013; Robitzsch, 2023). In applications, the expected sandwich (ESW) estimator evaluates A at ˆ︁ δ and, as an extension to incomplete administration patterns, estimates B separately for each administration pattern 𝑝 = 1, . . . , 𝑃. The 𝐼 𝑝 items that share an administration pattern 𝑝 also share the matrix L 𝑖 , which depends on the linking method and on the administration pattern (Eq. 8), so their estimating functions vary across these items with the same covariance matrix L 𝑖 𝚽L ⊤ 𝑖 . From here on, the hat denotes the finite-sample estimate, and g 𝑖 = g( ˆ︁ δ; ˆ︁ γ 𝑖 ) is the estimating function of item 𝑖 evaluated at the estimates. For each pattern 𝑝, the covariance matrix L 𝑖 𝚽L ⊤ 𝑖 is estimated by the empirical covariance matrix of the g 𝑖 of its items around their pattern mean ḡ𝑝 = 𝐼 -1 𝑝 ∑︁ 𝑖∈𝑝 g 𝑖 .

The meat matrix B is then estimated by ∑︁ 𝑝 𝐼 𝑝 ˆ︁ 𝚺 𝑝 . The observed sandwich instead inserts ˆ︁ A at ˆ︁ δ and the observed meat matrix ˆ︁ into the sandwich variance (Eq. 7) (Stefanski & Boos, 2002).

Each item contributes the outer product g 𝑖 g ⊤ 𝑖 of its estimating function, the matrix of all products of its components, so ˆ︁ B is computed directly from the data and needs neither administration patterns nor an estimate of 𝚽.

Because the estimating functions sum to zero at ˆ︁ δ (Eq. 4), ˆ︁ B measures the spread around a center that is itself estimated. Like a sample variance with the denominator 𝐼 instead of 𝐼 -1, the resulting sandwich variance tends to underestimate the LE variance (Fay & Graubard, 2001; Li & Redden, 2015). To correct this underestimation, the bias-corrected observed sandwich (BOSW) multiplies the observed sandwich variance by the finite-item factor 𝐼/(𝐼 -1) (Zeileis et al., 2020), a correction distinct from the person-sampling corrections in the Bias-Corrected

Linking Error Estimators subsection. The item jackknife (JK; e.g., Haberman et al., 2009; Monseur & Berezner, 2007; cf. Battauz, 2017) estimates the LE from recomputed linkings alone and needs neither the bread matrix A nor an estimate of the meat matrix B. Each recomputation deletes one common item and recomputes the complete linking from the remaining items without repeating the separate calibrations. The uncertainty of all links thus enters every recomputation, which is required for coverage close to the nominal level (Sachse & Haag, 2017). Because the target quantity ℎ is evaluated directly, no delta method is needed. With the delete-one estimate ˆ︁ ℎ (-𝑖)

Unlike the classical jackknife (Efron & Tibshirani, 1994), this estimator centers the differences at the estimate from all items rather than at the mean of the delete-one estimates and replaces the classical factor (𝐼 -1)/𝐼 by 𝐼/(𝐼 -1), which yielded more satisfactory coverage rates (Robitzsch, 2025b). The size of the factor replacement is visible for an arithmetic mean over the 𝐼 items, where the classical jackknife reproduces the BOSW exactly, whereas the factor 𝐼/(𝐼 -1) yields 𝐼 2 /(𝐼 -1) 2 times the BOSW variance, a multiplier that approaches one as 𝐼 grows. Among the item-resampling methods, the JK is used here because its 𝐼 deleteone recomputations involve no random resampling, so the same data always yield the same LE estimate, and because a person-sampling bias correction exists for its delete-one contrasts (Robitzsch, 2025b).

Standard Error

In a finite person sample, the calibrated item parameters ˆ︁ γ 𝑖 differ from their population values γ 𝑖 , the infinite-sample values of Equation (2), by sampling error, which the estimating equations transmit into the estimate ˆ︁ δ (e.g., Andersson, 2018; Battauz, 2013; Ogasawara, 2001). A firstorder Taylor expansion of g(δ; γ 𝑖 ) in the calibrated item parameters represents this transmission as a linear function of the sampling errors ˆ︁ γ 𝑖γ 𝑖 (e.g., Kolen & Brennan, 2014; Ogasawara, 2000), weighted by the derivative matrix g γ = ∂g/∂γ ⊤ 𝑖 of item 𝑖. The calibrated item parameters of all common items, stacked item by item into one vector ˆ︁ γ, have the sampling covariance matrix V ˆ︁ γ . On its diagonal, the within-item blocks V ˆ︁ γ 𝑖 collect the sampling covariances among the parameters of item 𝑖 across its time points. Off the diagonal, the between-item blocks V ˆ︁ γ 𝑖 ˆ︁ γ 𝑗 = Cov(ˆ︁ γ 𝑖 , ˆ︁ γ 𝑗 ) with 𝑖 ≠ 𝑗 are nonzero even under independent person samples, because within a time point all items are calibrated in the same person sample, so the sampling error of this person sample affects the calibrated item parameters ˆ︁ 𝑎 𝑖𝑡 and ˆ︁ 𝑏 𝑖𝑡 of all items at that time point together (Yuan et al., 2014). In applications, the sampling covariance matrix V ˆ︁ γ is replaced by its estimate ˆ︁ V ˆ︁ γ from the separate calibrations, with the blocks ˆ︁ V ˆ︁ γ 𝑖 ˆ︁ γ 𝑗 .

The variance of the sum of the weighted sampling errors g γ (δ; γ 𝑖 ) (ˆ︁ γ 𝑖γ 𝑖 ) over the items is LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS the full sampling meat matrix D, estimated by

All time points enter through the blocks of ˆ︁ V ˆ︁ γ , and because these blocks shrink as the person samples grow, the SE decreases with the person sample sizes, unlike the LE.

Bias-Corrected Linking Error Estimators

In finite person samples, each LE estimator contains a person-sampling share in addition to the item-selection variability that defines the LE (Haberman et al., 2009; Monseur & Berezner, 2007). The term bias-corrected refers here to the removal of the person-sampling share, not to the finite-item factor of the BOSW, and the bias-corrected LE is denoted LE bc . The origin of the person-sampling share is derived for the observed meat matrix ˆ︁

Each estimating function g 𝑖 carries the IPD vector o 𝑖 of its item and the sampling error ˆ︁ γ 𝑖γ 𝑖 of its calibrated item parameters. Because the sampling error has mean zero regardless of the IPD effects of the item, the two are uncorrelated, and the expectation of ˆ︁ B is the meat matrix B of the IPD effects (Eq. 8) plus the person-sampling share. In the sandwich estimators, the person-sampling share is estimated by the item-diagonal sampling meat matrix which keeps only the terms with 𝑖 = 𝑗 of the double sum in ˆ︁ D (Eq. 11), because ˆ︁ B contains one outer product per item and, to first order, no between-item terms.

Following Robitzsch (2024b), subtracting ˜︁ D gives the bias-corrected meat matrix ˆ︁ B bc , which replaces ˆ︁ B in the BOSW and gives the bias-corrected LE variance of the BOSW,

Because the difference of the positive semidefinite matrices ˆ︁ B and ˜︁ D need not be positive semidefinite, a negative LE variance of a target quantity is set to zero, as person sampling then explains the variability across items alone (Cronbach et al., 1972). For the target quantities of this article, this truncation suffices. The ESW requires the same subtraction, because its patternspecific covariance matrices ˆ︁ 𝚺 𝑝 also contain the person-sampling share. Only the finite-item factor 𝐼/(𝐼 -1) is not needed there, because each empirical covariance matrix ˆ︁ 𝚺 𝑝 is already computed with the denominator 𝐼 𝑝 -1, and this factor concerns the estimated center, not the LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS person-sampling share. Because the center is estimated, the subtraction slightly overcorrects when the sampling errors of the calibrated item parameters are positively correlated across items or the number of items is small (cf. Robitzsch, 2024b). The JK is corrected with the same logic. The delete-one contrasts ˆ︁ ℎ (-𝑖)ℎ( ˆ︁ δ) of Equation (10) are linearized with respect to the calibrated item parameters, and the person-sampling share ˆ︁ β JK of the squared JK LE is subtracted, ˆ︂ LE 2 JK,bc = ˆ︂ LE 2 JK -ˆ︁ β JK , again truncated at zero (Robitzsch, 2024b (Robitzsch, , 2025b)). Unlike the item-diagonal sampling meat matrix ˜︁ D, the personsampling share ˆ︁ β JK uses the full sampling covariance matrix ˆ︁ V ˆ︁ γ , because every delete-one contrast depends on the calibrated item parameters of all remaining items. The gradients of the delete-one contrasts follow from the implicit function theorem through the bread matrix ˆ︁ A and the derivative matrices g γ (Eqs. S1 and S2). The two subtractions of ˜︁ D and ˆ︁ β JK rest on the same linearization in the calibrated item parameters, as jackknife variance estimators are asymptotically equivalent to sandwich estimators for estimating equations (Boos & Stefanski, 2013; Lipsitz et al., 1994; Shao, 1992).

Total Error

Person sampling and item selection are assumed to be independent random mechanisms, so the expansion of the estimation error ˆ︁ δδ splits into a person-sampling part and an item-selection part whose cross products have zero expectation, just as the sampling error and the IPD effects in the observed meat matrix ˆ︁ B are uncorrelated. The TE variance is then the sum of the SE variance V SE and the LE variance V LE (Michaelides & Haertel, 2014; Xu & von Davier, 2010), the sandwich variances (Eq. 7) with the sampling meat matrix D and with the meat matrix B of the IPD effects, respectively,

LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS

For dependent samples, V ˆ︁ γ is estimated by a stacked calibration or by a person bootstrap. The stacked calibration treats the 𝑇 separate calibrations as one M-estimation problem in which the persons are the independent units. The estimating functions are the calibration scores, the derivatives of each person's marginal log-likelihood contribution with respect to the item parameters (Eqs. S3 to S5). The bread matrix of the stacked calibration is block diagonal, with one block per separate calibration (Eq. S4), so the dependence between time points enters only through the off-diagonal blocks of its meat matrix (Eq. S5), which sum the products of the calibration scores of the shared persons at two time points. The person bootstrap draws samples of size 𝑁 ∪ with replacement from the union sample and keeps each person's complete responses and participation pattern z 𝑛 = (𝑧 𝑛1 , . . . , 𝑧 𝑛𝑇 ) ⊤ . Each replicate is recalibrated at every time point, and V ˆ︁ γ is estimated by the empirical covariance matrix of the calibrated item parameters across the 𝑅 boot replicates (Efron & Tibshirani, 1994).

The stacked calibration and the person bootstrap assume that participation does not depend on the abilities (Rubin, 1976). Selective nonresponse biases the calibrated item parameters themselves and is not handled in this treatment.

Because the abilities of the shared persons are typically positively correlated over time, so are the sampling errors of the calibrated item parameters at different time points. The estimating functions contrast the calibrated item parameters of the same item at two time points, such as log ˆ︁ 𝑎 𝑖2log ˆ︁ 𝑎 𝑖1 , so the correlated sampling errors partly cancel in these differences. Treating dependent samples as independent therefore tends to overstate the SE (Jewsbury, 2025b; Kolen & Brennan, 2014; Liou & Cheng, 1995). The understatement often expected under ignored dependence concerns sums of positively correlated errors instead, such as those accumulating along a chain of links (Guo, 2010). Through the subtraction of ˜︁ D (Eq. 14), the same assumption tends to understate LE bc , although the direction follows the signs of the estimated cross-timepoint covariances and is not guaranteed in general.

Mean-Geometric Mean and Pairwise Haberman Linking for Three Time Points

The following subsections derive closed-form expressions, referred to as the closed forms, for the true LE, that is, the LE with infinite person samples. The closed forms hold for any zeromean IPD process, whereas the LE estimators do not depend on the IPD process. Because the closed forms carry the cross-link covariances of the IPD effects as free quantities, the random walk is only the special case in which these covariances are zero (Eq. S8). For each linking method, the closed forms follow from the estimating functions g with infinite person samples. The closed forms are given for the linked T3 parameters µ 3 and σ 3 , to which both links contribute. The derivative matrices for the SE and the person-sampling bias corrections are given in Equations ( S6) and (S7). The closed forms and the sampling meat matrices were verified symbolically with the computer algebra system Yacas through the R package

Ryacas (Andersen & Højsgaard, 2019; Pinkus & Winitzki, 2002) and confirmed numerically with infinite person samples. The verification scripts are available with the Supplement at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.34092000.v1.

LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS

Common-Item Design

For three time points, T1, T2, and T3, the common items fall into three common-item sets (Figure 1). The set 𝐶 1:3 contains the items administered at all three time points, 𝐶 1:2 those administered at T1 and T2 only, and 𝐶 2:3 those administered at T2 and T3 only. From the administration indicators 𝑑 𝑖𝑡 , the common-item indicators 𝑑 𝑖,12 , 𝑑 𝑖,23 , and 𝑑 𝑖,123 and the commonitem counts are T1 T2 T3 Contribution 𝐶 1:3 𝐶 1:3 𝐶 1:3 T1 ↔ T2 and T2 ↔ T3 links 𝐶 1:2 𝐶 1:2 T1 ↔ T2 link only 𝐶 2:3 𝐶 2:3 T2 ↔ T3 link only Note. Shaded cells indicate that a common-item set is administered at the corresponding time point.

Mean-Geometric Mean Linking

MGM (Kolen & Brennan, 2014; Mislevy & Bock, 1990) links consecutive time points through the geometric mean of the item discriminations and the mean of the rescaled item difficulties.

With the log SDs s 𝑡 , the T1 ↔ T2 link yields the mean µ 2 and SD σ 2 of T2 directly on the T1 scale, which the T1 calibration fixes through µ1 = 0 and σ1 = 1, where ˆ︁ σ2 = exp (ˆ︁ s 2 ), and the T2 ↔ T3 link yields the link-specific mean µ 2,3 and SD σ 2,3 of T3 on the T2 scale in the same way.

With s 2,3 = log σ 2,3 , chain linking combines both links on the T1 scale through µ3 = µ 2 + σ 2 µ 2,3 and s3 = s 2 + s 2,3 (e.g., Battauz, 2013), and its parameters LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS are collected in δ = (s 2 , µ 2 , s 2,3 , µ 2,3 ) ⊤ , which contains the parameters of the two links rather than the linked T3 parameters. The MGM estimate of δ solves the estimating equations ( Eq. 4)with the estimating function of item 𝑖

At the true parameter vector δ, the identities (Eq. 2) and the definition of the IPD effects (Eq. 3) reduce the estimating function to g(δ; γ 𝑖 ) = (︁ 𝑑 𝑖,12 𝑓 𝑖2 , 𝑑 𝑖,12 𝑒 𝑖2 , 𝑑 𝑖,23 𝑓 𝑖3 , 𝑑 𝑖,23 σ -1 2 𝑒 𝑖3 )︁ ⊤ , where the factor σ -1 2 arises because the T2 ↔ T3 link works on the T2 scale, whereas 𝑒 𝑖3 is defined on the T1 scale.

Because the IPD effects have zero means, all four components have expectation zero, and MGM is consistent for the parameters in δ as the number of items grows (Robitzsch, 2021). The linearization (Eq. 6), combined with the delta method (Eq. 9) for these chain-linking relations, represents the estimation errors ˆ︁ s 3s 3 and ˆ︁ µ 3µ 3 of the linked T3 parameters as sums of the IPD effects of the items, with the offsets Δ12 = µ 3 -b12 and Δ23 = µ 3 -b23 between the T3 mean and the mean item difficulties of the two links on the T1 scale.

Every item enters a link with the same coefficient, or error weight, 1/𝐼 12 or 1/𝐼 23 , and the items of 𝐶 1:3 enter both links. The difficulty IPD effects 𝑒 𝑖𝑡 shift the linked mean directly, whereas the discrimination IPD effects 𝑓 𝑖𝑡 distort the estimated SDs, which stretch the scale of the item difficulties and move the linked mean in proportion to the offset Δ 12 or Δ 23 . The LEs are the SDs of the sums in Equation ( 20). For σ 3 , this gives which contains only discrimination IPD effects, because the item difficulties do not enter the estimation of the log SD parameters.

The LE of the linked T3 mean is

The terms with the denominators 𝐼 12 and 𝐼 23 are the contributions of the two links, and the second line is the cross-link contribution of the shared items in 𝐶 1:3 , weighted by both error weights.

Pairwise Haberman Linking

Unlike MGM chain linking, PHL estimates δ = (s 2 , s 3 , µ 2 , µ 3 ) ⊤ , in which all entries are linked parameters on the T1 scale, simultaneously from all time-point pairs (Haberman, 2009; Robitzsch, 2025a). 𝑖 for the item difficulties. Because the original method estimates these joint item parameters together with the linked parameters, the number of its estimated parameters grows with the number of items, whereas M-estimation theory requires a parameter vector of fixed length (Boos & Stefanski, 2013). In the difference between the two time points of a time-point pair, the joint item parameters log 𝑎 * 𝑖 and 𝑏 * 𝑖 cancel, which leads to the following pairwise criteria, and PHL coincides with the original method when all common items are administered at all time points (Robitzsch, 2025a). With the item weights ω 𝑖 and the square loss 𝑥 2 /2 (Robitzsch, 2025a), the criteria for the vectors s = (s 2 , s 3 ) ⊤ and µ = (µ 2 , µ 3 ) ⊤ are where the common-item indicator 𝑑 𝑖,𝑡𝑡 ′ = 𝑑 𝑖𝑡 𝑑 𝑖𝑡 ′ selects the time-point pairs at which item 𝑖 is administered, in the present design the items of 𝐶 1:3 for the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3.

Because the criteria depend only on differences between time points, the reference scale has to be set explicitly, and µ1 = 0 and s1 = 0, the log form of σ1 = 1, set it to the T1 scale.

The item weights ω 𝑖 determine how strongly each item enters the criteria. With unit item weights, ω 𝑖 = 1, an item administered at 𝑚 𝑖 = ∑︁ 3 𝑡=1 𝑑 𝑖𝑡 time points contributes 𝑚 𝑖 (𝑚 𝑖 -1)/2 pairwise differences per criterion, so items administered at more time points weigh more. The item weights ω 𝑖 = 𝐼/𝑚 𝑖 reduce this influence and keep PHL close to the original Haberman linking (Robitzsch, 2025a). S12), with ˜︁ 𝐼 123 and 𝐽 123 for the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3. With unit item weights, both reduce to the common-item counts 𝐼 𝑡𝑡 ′ (Eq. 17). The factor 𝐼 in ω 𝑖 = 𝐼/𝑚 𝑖 enters A linearly and B quadratically, so it cancels in every sandwich variance, and only the ratios of the item weights matter. The estimating functions are the item contributions to the derivatives of the criteria, with a negative sign for the log SDs and a positive sign for the LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS means, so that both take the same form in Equation ( 24). Within each link, the error weights of one IPD effect sum to one, so the estimation error ˆ︁ s 3s 3 is again a weighted average of discrimination IPD effects, and MGM is the special case of the equal error weights λ 𝑖 = (𝑑 𝑖,12 /𝐼 12 , 𝑑 𝑖,23 /𝐼 23 ) ⊤ in Equation ( 20). Taking the SD of this weighted average gives the LE of the linked T3 SD, where the three terms are the contributions of 𝐶 1:3 , 𝐶 1:2 , and 𝐶 2:3 .

Comparison and Special Cases

The two linking methods differ in the error weights. MGM gives all items of a link the same error weight. PHL gives the items of 𝐶 1:3 larger error weights, because only these items are administered at both T1 and T3 and thus enter the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3, and the item weights ω 𝑖 = 𝐼/𝑚 𝑖 shrink this imbalance without removing it. By the definition of the IPD effects (Eq. 3), the difference of the calibrated item parameters of an item of 𝐶 1:3 between T1 and T3 equals the sum of its differences in the two links, so the direct time-point pair carries the sums 𝑓 𝑖2 + 𝑓 𝑖3 and 𝑒 𝑖2 + 𝑒 𝑖3 of the IPD effects of both links and adds no information beyond the links.

Which of the two methods yields the smaller true LE depends on the cross-link covariances τ 𝑓 2 𝑓 3 and τ 𝑒 2 𝑒 3 , the covariances of the IPD effects of the same item in the two links. If they are zero, as under the random walk, equal error weights within each link minimize the variance of the estimation error ˆ︁ s 3s3 ≈ ∑︁ 𝑖 λ ⊤ 𝑖 f 𝑖 . The true LE of ˆ︁ σ 3 is then smaller under MGM, and so is that of ˆ︁ µ 3 under uniform IPD (cf. Engels et al., 2026a). PHL yields the smaller true LE in this design only if the cross-link covariances are sufficiently negative, as under administration-specific effects that do not accumulate (Eq. S9).

Under uniform IPD or in the 1PL model, all discrimination IPD effects and their covariances vanish. For both linking methods, LE(ˆ︁ σ 3 ) = 0, the offset terms drop out, and LE(ˆ︁ µ 3 ) takes the form of Equation ( 21) or (26) with σ3 = 1 and the difficulty IPD effects in place of the discrimination IPD effects. The cross-link covariance τ 𝑒 2 𝑒 3 of the difficulty IPD effects then enters LE(ˆ︁ µ 3 ) through the items of 𝐶 1:3 , which belong to both links. If it is positive, the two difficulty IPD effects of such an item tend to point in the same direction and add up, so the LE increases. If it is negative, they partly cancel, and the LE decreases.

MGM and PHL yield the same estimates in three special cases (Engels et al., 2025). With two time points, PHL coincides with MGM (Eqs. S29 and S30; Haberman, 2009; Mislevy and Bock, 1990). With three time points, the two methods coincide if no item is administered at all three time points, because the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3 is then empty, and if every common item is administered at all three time points, because every time-point pair then rests on the same items. In these two limiting cases, the closed forms (Eqs. S25 to S28) and the LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS sandwich estimators of the LE coincide as well.

With dependent person samples, the two methods also differ in how the shared persons of T1 and T3 enter the bias correction. For PHL, the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3 adds the sampling covariance of ˆ︁ 𝑎 𝑖1 and ˆ︁ 𝑎 𝑖3 , which arises from these shared persons, to the item-diagonal sampling meat matrix ˜︁ D, for example to its entry ˜︁ 𝐷 s 3 s 3 for the linked T3 log SD (Eq. S35). For MGM, this sampling covariance enters ˜︁ D only through the cross entries between the parameters of the first and the second link, for example ˜︁ 𝐷 s 2 s 2,3 (Eq. S33).

Simulation Study Method

For MGM and PHL, the simulation study examined how well the LE estimators recover the item-selection variability and whether the bias corrections remove the person-sampling share from the LE estimates. The study also examined the coverage of the intervals based on the SE, the TE, and TE bc . On the T1 scale, with µ1 = 0 and σ1 = 1, the means of the later time points were µ2 = 0.3 and µ3 = 0.5 and their SDs σ2 = 1.2 and σ3 = 1.5, which represents growth in the mean and an increasing spread of the abilities (e.g., Student et al., 2025).

The common items followed the design in Figure 1, with 5, 10, or 15 items in each of the common-item sets 𝐶 1:3 , 𝐶 1:2 , and 𝐶 2:3 , so that 𝐼 = 15, 30, or 45, 𝐼12 = 𝐼23 = 2𝐼/3, and 𝐼123 = 𝐼/3. Each common-item set consisted of a base set of five items, used once, twice, or three times (Table S1), so that the number of items varied while the distribution of the item parameters stayed the same. The mean item difficulties of the three base sets were 0.25 (𝐶 1:3 ), 0.05 (𝐶 1:2 ), and 0.44 (𝐶 2:3 ), close to the mean abilities of the time points each set spans, and the respective mean item discriminations were 0.94, 1.08, and 0.91.

The person samples per time point were infinite or of size 𝑁 = 500, 1000, or 2000 (Harwell et al., 1996). The four IPD effects of every item, the entries of its IPD vector o 𝑖 , were drawn independently of each other and across items, with zero means and the IPD SDs τ 𝑒 for the difficulty and τ 𝑓 for the discrimination IPD effects in both links. These IPD SDs were τ 𝑒 = 0.25 and τ 𝑓 = 0.125 at the weak and τ 𝑒 = 0.5 and τ 𝑓 = 0.25 at the strong IPD level (Engels et al., 2025), and zero in the condition without IPD, in which the true LE is zero. All covariances in 𝚽 were thus zero, so the item parameters followed the random walk (Eq. 3) from the first administration of each item onward, and the items of 𝐶 2:3 received their first IPD effects at T3. The IPD effects were drawn from normal distributions or, with heavier tails at the same variances, from 𝑡 distributions with three degrees of freedom (𝑡 3 ), scaled by √︁ 1/3. The condition without IPD and the two IPD levels under each of the two distributions gave five IPD conditions. Crossed with the three numbers of items and the four sample sizes, they yielded 60 cells. Every cell used 𝑅 = 4000 replications, with the IPD effects redrawn in each replication, which puts the Monte Carlo standard error of a coverage rate at the nominal level at 0.34 percentage points (Morris et al., 2019). In each replication, the baseline item parameters 𝑎 𝑖 and 𝑏 𝑖 of every item were those of Table S1, and the drawn IPD effects shifted them at the later administrations of the item (Eq. 3). With infinite person samples, the calibrated item LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS parameters were set to their population values (Eq. 2) (cf. Robitzsch, 2024b), and the empirical SD of the linked estimates across the replications of a cell served as the true LE. With finite person samples, independent person samples were drawn at each time point 𝑡 from N(µ 𝑡 , σ 2 𝑡 ), and the item responses were generated from the 2PL model. Each time point was then calibrated separately by marginal maximum likelihood with the expectation-maximization algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981), under the identifying restriction θ ∼ N(0, 1) and with the estimated item discriminations bounded below at 0.1, so that near-zero estimates do not produce extreme log item discriminations in the links.

MGM was applied as chain linking and PHL with the item weights ω 𝑖 = 𝐼/𝑚 𝑖 . For all four linked parameters, µ 2 , σ 2 , µ 3 , and σ 3 , the ESW, the BOSW, and the JK were computed in every replication. With finite person samples, the SE, the LE bc estimates, the TE, and TE bc were added. The linked estimates were evaluated by their bias and root mean square error (RMSE) across the replications. LE estimates were summarized by cell medians rather than means, because LE estimates, as SDs computed from few items, were right-skewed within a cell, and an LE bc estimate is set to zero whenever the bias correction yields a negative LE variance. With infinite person samples, the recovery of the item-selection variability was assessed by the ratio of the median LE estimate in a cell to the true LE of the cell, with the ideal value one (Morris et al., 2019). With finite person samples, the median LE estimate in a cell was compared with its median under infinite person samples in the same IPD condition and with the same number of common items. This difference isolates the person-sampling share, and absolute differences above 0.01 are marked in the tables.

Coverage was evaluated for the 95% intervals of the linked parameters, formed by the linked estimate ±1.96 times its LE estimate (infinite person samples) or its estimated SE, TE, or TE bc (finite person samples). Coverage rates between 92.5% and 97.5% were classified as acceptable, based on the rates rounded to one decimal place as they are reported. A variance decomposition of the binary indicator of unacceptable coverage, which treats undercoverage and overcoverage alike, quantified the shares of the simulation factors and their interactions (Table S17), and Figure 2 shows all coverage rates of the TE-and TE bc -based intervals for ˆ︁ µ 3 and ˆ︁ σ 3 as a specification curve (Simonsohn et al., 2020).

The Results focus on the linked T3 parameters µ 3 and σ 3 , because T3 is the time point most distant from T1 and its linked parameters rest on both links. The tables for ˆ︁ σ 3 , the T2 results, and the ˆ︁ µ 3 cells with strong 𝑡 3 IPD are given in the Supplement, and statements about all cells include them. All analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.5.2; R Core Team, 2025) with the package irtlink (Engels, 2026), which implements the calibration, the linking methods, and all LE, SE, and TE estimators.

Results

Linked Estimates

MGM and PHL recovered µ 3 and σ 3 with small bias (Table S3). Because the consistency of MGM and PHL refers to the number of items (Eqs. 19 and 24), a finite-item bias remains with effects, for example, of ˆ︁ σ3 = exp (ˆ︁ s 3 ) in the discrimination IPD effects. The largest absolute bias occurred for ˆ︁ σ 3 under strong normal IPD at 𝐼 = 15, with 0.013 under MGM and 0.014 under PHL with infinite person samples and 0.031 and 0.033 at 𝑁 = 500.

Table 1 shows that the RMSE of ˆ︁ µ 3 with infinite person samples decreased with the number of items and was larger under PHL than under MGM in every cell, as the closed forms imply for zero cross-link covariances (cf. Engels et al., 2026a). Because the bias was small, this RMSE nearly equaled the empirical SD of the linked estimates, that is, the true LE. Table S2 shows that, with finite person samples, the RMSE also decreased with 𝑁 toward its value with infinite person samples, except for ˆ︁ µ 3 under strong 𝑡 3 IPD at 𝐼 = 15, where single replications with extreme IPD draws dominated the RMSE. For ˆ︁ σ 3 with infinite person samples, the RMSE was likewise larger under PHL in every cell, most clearly at 𝐼 = 15 under weak 𝑡 3 IPD (0.106 versus 0.092), where the estimation errors under PHL had heavier tails (Table S6).

Linking Error Estimates With Infinite Person Samples

With infinite person samples, the LE estimates reflect item selection alone. Table 1 relates the median LE estimates for ˆ︁ µ 3 to the true LE. For the JK, this ratio ranged from 1.00 to 1.08 under the normal distribution, highest at 𝐼 = 15 in line with the factor 𝐼/(𝐼 -1) of Equation ( 10), and from 0.86 to 0.92 under the scaled 𝑡 3 distribution. Heavy IPD tails strengthen the right skew of the LE estimates, so a single data set then typically yields an estimate below the true LE, whereas the ratio of the mean JK estimate to the true LE ranged from 0.96 to 1.00 (Table S11).

The ratios of the ESW and the BOSW lay below those of the JK in every cell, most at 𝐼 = 15, and below one even under the normal distribution. At 𝐼 = 15, where each link had ten items, the gap under MGM was close to the factor 10/9 by which the JK exceeds the BOSW for a mean over ten items (Eq. 10), for example, 1.07 versus 0.96 under weak normal IPD. Under PHL, the LE estimates varied more across replications, with a larger interquartile range of the JK estimates for ˆ︁ µ 3 and ˆ︁ σ 3 than under MGM in every cell (Table S10), and their ratios to the true LE were lower than under MGM, most clearly at 𝐼 = 15, consistent with the concentration of the error weights λ 𝑖 on the items of 𝐶 1:3 (Eq. 25). For ˆ︁ σ 3 , the JK ratio ranged from 0.99 to 1.06 under the normal distribution and from 0.72 to 0.92 under the scaled 𝑡 3 distribution (Table S6).

Linking Error Estimates With Finite Person Samples

Table 2 shows that person sampling inflates the uncorrected LE estimates for ˆ︁ µ 3 relative to their reference, the median under infinite person samples. Without IPD, the true LE is zero, but the median uncorrected estimates lay far above zero and decreased with 𝑁 at the 1/ √ 𝑁 rate of the SE. With IPD, the median uncorrected JK LE exceeded its reference in every cell, by more than 0.01 in all cells at 𝑁 = 500 and in two cells at 𝑁 = 2000, most strongly under weak IPD, for example, 0.165 versus 0.121 under weak normal IPD at 𝐼 = 15 and 𝑁 = 500. The uncorrected sandwich estimators behaved alike, and PHL and MGM differed little. The bias corrections removed the person-sampling share. Without IPD, all bias-corrected medians were zero, so the truncation at zero applied in at least half of the replications. With IPD, the median LE bc of the JK stayed within 0.01 of its reference in all cells, for example, 0.116, 0.121, and 0.120 at the three sample sizes in the same condition. The bias-corrected sandwich estimators overcorrected at 𝐼 = 15, with deviations above 0.01 mainly at 𝑁 = 500 and none at 𝑁 = 2000. For ˆ︁ σ 3 , whose true LE was small relative to the SE, the uncorrected medians deviated more, and the bias corrections overcorrected somewhat more often at 𝐼 = 15 (Table S12). Coverage Figure 2 gives an overview of all 1080 coverage rates of the TE-and TE bc -based intervals for ˆ︁ µ 3 and ˆ︁ σ 3 with finite person samples as a specification curve (Simonsohn et al., 2020). Most rates, 871, lay within the acceptable range. Of the 45 undercovered specifications on the left, 44 had 𝐼 = 15, 44 used a sandwich estimator, 42 used the bias correction, and 40 belonged to PHL, whereas all 164 overcovered specifications on the right used no bias correction and most of them had no or weak IPD. In the variance decomposition of unacceptable coverage, the interaction of the IPD condition with the bias correction accounted for the largest share (Table S17).

Table 3 gives the coverage rates for ˆ︁ µ 3 . With infinite person samples, the intervals based on the JK LE estimate reached acceptable coverage in all cells under both linking methods. with the ESW deviating less often than the BOSW (cf. Fay & Graubard, 2001). With finite person samples, the SE-based intervals reached the nominal level without IPD but undercovered in every cell with IPD, because the SE omits the LE, whose share of the TE grows with the sample size. Larger samples therefore aggravate this undercoverage. Under strong normal IPD at 𝐼 = 15, the coverage under MGM fell from 67.8% at 𝑁 = 500 to 39.9% at 𝑁 = 2000, whereas the interval based on the TE bc of the JK covered in 95.0% and 95.1%. The TE-based intervals overcovered wherever the true LE is small relative to the person-sampling share of the LE estimate, that is, in nearly all cells without IPD, with up to 99.2%, and in a few cells with weak IPD. Without IPD, the overcoverage decreased with the number of items but not with the sample size, because the person-sampling share and the SE shrink at the same rate. With the bias correction, this overcoverage disappeared. The intervals based on the TE bc of the JK stayed within the acceptable range in all cells, whereas those based on the TE bc of the sandwich estimators undercovered at 𝐼 = 15, mainly under PHL and down to 90.8%, in line with the overcorrection of their bias corrections. Under strong 𝑡 3 IPD, the results resembled those under strong normal IPD (Table S4). For ˆ︁ σ 3 , the intervals based on the ESW and the BOSW with infinite person samples also undercovered under MGM under strong normal IPD at 𝐼 = 15, and with finite person samples, the TE-based intervals overcovered more often, also in many cells with weak IPD. The intervals based on the TE bc of the JK stayed within the acceptable range in all but one cell (92.4% for PHL under strong normal IPD at 𝐼 = 15 and 𝑁 = 1000), and those based on the TE bc of the sandwich estimators undercovered down to 89.5% (Table S7).

Empirical Example Method

The estimators are illustrated with data from the Kompetenzen und Einstellungen von Schülerinnen und Schülern study (KESS; Bos et al., 2024; Guill et al., 2024; Vieluf et al., 2024), a longitudinal LSA conducted in Hamburg, Germany. The example uses the mathematics assessment of students in the academic track (Gymnasium) at the beginning of Grade 7 in 2005 (T1), the end of Grade 8 in 2007 (T2), and the beginning of Grade 11 in 2009 (T3). To protect participant confidentiality, the example uses a synthetic data set generated by data-augmented multiple imputation (Grund et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2022). The procedure imputes the responses by partial least squares regression and adds random noise with the noise parameter 0.3, so that the synthetic data retain the distributional structure of the original responses. Because the three time points followed one student cohort, the person samples were dependent. Of the 𝑁 ∪ = 6970 students of the union sample, 𝑁 𝑡 = 4521, 5263, and 5152 were assessed at T1, T2, and T3, and 2996 at all three time points. The numbers of shared persons were 𝑁12 = 3863, 𝑁23 = 3948, and 𝑁13 = 3151. Of the 139 mathematics items, 36 served as common items, with 12 in 𝐶 1:3 , 10 in 𝐶 1:2 , and 14 in 𝐶 2:3 , so that 𝐼12 = 22, 𝐼23 = 26, and 𝐼123 = 12 (Figure S1). The items were distributed across booklets in a multiple-matrix sampling design (Frey et al., 2009; Rutkowski et al., 2014), and each common item was answered by 1071 to 5263 students at a time point. The booklet design leaves the closed forms of the LE unchanged, because the linked estimates rest on the calibrated item parameters of all administered common items, regardless of which students answered them (Robitzsch, 2023). Separate calibration and linking followed the simulation study. The sampling covariance matrix V ˆ︁ γ of the calibrated item parameters, including its cross-time-point blocks, was estimated with the stacked calibration and with the person bootstrap with 𝑅 boot = 2000 replicates (Andrews & Buchinsky, 2000). For MGM and PHL, the three LE estimators were applied to µ 2 , σ 2 , µ 3 , and σ 3 . The SE was computed with the stacked calibration (SE st ), with the person bootstrap (SE boot ), and under the assumption of independent person samples (SE ind ), and each of the three entered its own TE and TE bc.

Results

All three separate calibrations and all 𝑅 boot = 2000 bootstrap recalibrations converged. Table S18 gives the linked item parameters of the common items under MGM and their differences between consecutive administrations. The differences of the item difficulties range from -1.15 to 1.65 and go in both directions, so individual items became easier as well as harder.

Table 4 reports the linked estimates with the three SEs, the three LE estimates, and the TEs and bias corrections based on the stacked calibration. Under MGM, the mathematics achievement of the cohort increased by ˆ︁ µ2 = 0.74 from Grade 7 to Grade 8 and by ˆ︁ µ3 = 1.40 from Grade 7 to Grade 11 on the T1 scale, while the SD remained close to one (ˆ︁ σ2 = 1.03, ︁ σ3 = 0.95). PHL gave slightly smaller growth estimates, ˆ︁ µ2 = 0.72 and ˆ︁ µ3 = 1.36, but the differences to MGM were small relative to the TE bc,st of the JK, which was 0.11 for ˆ︁ µ 2 and 0.18 for ˆ︁ µ 3 under MGM.

The LE estimates of all three estimators exceeded the SEs for all linked parameters. For ︁ µ 3 under MGM, the JK LE was 0.182, compared with an SE st of 0.048 and an SE boot of 0.050. At the given sample sizes, the uncertainty of the linked means was therefore dominated by the selection of the common items rather than by person sampling (Michaelides & Haertel, 2014). For ˆ︁ σ 2 and ˆ︁ σ 3 , the LE estimates were smaller in absolute terms but still about twice the SEs. The three LE estimates agreed closely, with the sandwich estimates slightly below the JK estimate, and the bias corrections reduced the LE estimates only modestly, because the large person samples imply a small person-sampling share of the variability across items. For ˆ︁ µ 3 under MGM, LE bc,st ranged from 0.168 (BOSW) to 0.177 (JK) and TE bc,st from 0.174 to 0.183, which gave 95% intervals of about 1.40 ± 0.35. Here, TE bc,st slightly exceeded the uncorrected LE estimate for all three estimators, so the SE added back more than the correction had removed, and the uncorrected TE st , 0.180 to 0.188, lay above both. For the sandwich estimators, this is consistent with positive between-item sampling covariances, which the SE contains (Eq. 11) but the item-diagonal correction (Eq. 13) omits.

The LE estimates of PHL exceeded those of MGM for all four parameters and all three estimators, for example, 0.213 versus 0.182 for the JK LE of ˆ︁ µ 3 . Under the random walk, this ordering is the expected one, and the differences of the linked item parameters between consecutive administrations indicate which IPD process the data support. For the 12 items of 𝐶 1:3 , the differences of the item difficulties in the two links were uncorrelated across items (𝑟 = .00), and those of the log item discriminations correlated LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS weakly positively (𝑟 = .31; Table S19). With 12 items, both values are only a rough check, but they are consistent with the random walk (Eq. 3) rather than with administration-specific effects, which would imply a correlation near -.5 (Eq. S9). S20 gives the total errors and the bias corrections for all three estimators of the sampling covariance matrix.

Treating the three person samples as independent overstated the SE, most visibly for ˆ︁ µ 2 (SE ind = 0.033 instead of SE st = 0.029 under MGM). The overstatement remained moderate, because the estimated cross-time-point covariances of the calibrated item parameters were small relative to their variances. The abilities of the shared persons, estimated as expected a posteriori scores, correlated .54 to .59 between time points, whereas the sampling errors of the calibrated item parameters showed median cross-time-point correlations of only .01 to .05. SE st and SE boot differed by at most 0.001 for all linked parameters except ˆ︁ µ 3 , for which SE boot was 0.050 and 0.048 instead of 0.048 and 0.045 under MGM and PHL (Table 4). This difference originates in the covariance estimates themselves rather than in the linearization of the linked estimates with respect to the calibrated item parameters, because the SE computed from the bootstrap covariance agreed within 1% with the SE computed directly from the replicates of the linked estimates. The TEs and the bias corrections computed with the bootstrap or the independence covariance differed from their stacked counterparts by at most 0.001 (Table S20).

Discussion

This article cast MGM and PHL as M-estimation problems for any number of time points and derived the LE, the SE, and the TE of the linked means and SDs, together with bias corrections for person sampling and an extension to dependent person samples. The closed forms make the role of the cross-link covariances of the IPD effects explicit, and the simulation compared the two linking methods and the three LE estimators under the same conditions.

With infinite person samples, the JK reached acceptable coverage in all cells, whereas the sandwich estimators undercovered at the smallest number of common items, more strongly under PHL. With finite person samples, the bias corrections removed the person-sampling share from the LE estimates, and the intervals based on the TE bc of the JK reached acceptable coverage in all cells but one. The bias corrections of the sandwich estimators overcorrected at 𝐼 = 15, so their intervals undercovered there, consistent with the between-item sampling terms that the item-diagonal correction omits. The SE-based intervals undercovered in every condition with IPD, and this undercoverage grew with the sample size (Monseur & Berezner, 2007; Wu, 2010).

In the empirical example, the LE estimates exceeded the SEs for all linked parameters, and those of PHL exceeded those of MGM, most strongly for ˆ︁ µ 3 . Under equal IPD variances and zero cross-link covariances, the closed forms predict an excess of only about 5% in this design (Eqs. 21, 22, 26, and 27). The remainder cannot be separated from the variability of the LE estimates in a single data set, which the simulation showed to be larger under PHL. Because the IPD process of an assessment is unknown, the choice between the linking methods implies an assumption about this process. Under the random walk, MGM yields the smaller LE in this design. PHL can yield the smaller LE when the cross-link covariances are sufficiently negative (Eq. S9), and it gains relative to MGM with items that skip T2, which only the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3 uses, and when person sampling dominates, because this time-point pair is free of the sampling error of the T2 calibration.

The simulation used one connected design with common-item sets of equal size, normal ability distributions, equal sample sizes at all time points, and IPD effects with zero covariances. Common-item sets of unequal size and unequal sample sizes across time points, as they arise from attrition in longitudinal studies, are next steps, because both the number of common items and the sample size affect the variability of chained equating coefficients (cf. Battauz, 2015). IPD processes with nonzero cross-link covariances are a further step, for which the closed forms indicate where differences between the linking methods should appear. Samples smaller than those studied here, such as 𝑁 = 250, raise the person-sampling share of the variation across items, so the bias corrections and the truncation at zero matter more and need their own evaluation. The extension to dependent person samples was illustrated but not evaluated by simulation. Varying the numbers 𝑁 𝑡𝑡 ′ of shared persons and the correlation of the abilities across time points would show how far the stacked calibration and the person bootstrap recover the SE and LE bc.

LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS

The SE treated the students as independent draws, although they are nested in schools. Summing the calibration scores of the students within schools in the meat matrix of the stacked calibration (Eq. S5), as in cluster-robust sandwich estimators (Liang & Zeger, 1986), or using replication weights (Wu, 2010) would typically enlarge the SE. The uncorrected LE estimates would not change, because they use only the calibrated item parameters. The M-estimation framework also assumes IPD effects that are independent across items. If IPD is also a property of the testlet for items that share a stimulus (Monseur et al., 2008; Wainer et al., 2007), the testlet replaces the item as the independent unit, so the meat matrix sums over testlets and the JK deletes one testlet at a time (Monseur & Berezner, 2007). Finally, the decomposition of the TE into the SE and the LE rests on the independence of item selection and person sampling, which is not guaranteed when test forms are assigned by prior achievement or in adaptive testing, where the administered items depend on the abilities of the assessed persons (Fink et al., 2025).

Under the three-and four-parameter logistic models, the guessing and slipping parameters are unaffected by linear transformations of the ability scale (Kolen & Brennan, 2014; Loken & Rulison, 2010), and under the graded response model (Samejima, 1969), the estimating functions collect several thresholds per item, so the derivations carry over. Beyond the item weights, the criteria of PHL could weight the time-point pairs, for example, with weights that decrease with the distance between the time points, which would down-weight the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3, whose items carry the sums of the IPD effects of both links. Mean-mean linking fits the same M-estimation framework (Loyd & Hoover, 1980), but because the random walk (Eq. 3) acts on the log item discriminations, it holds their geometric rather than their arithmetic mean constant, which matches MGM.

Model misspecification, including nonnormal ability distributions, leaves the decomposition of the TE valid for pseudo-true parameters (White, 1982), and simulations with a datagenerating model more complex than the 2PL analysis model, such as a model with asymmetric IRFs (Lee & Bolt, 2018; Liao & Bolt, 2021; Samejima, 2000), would show how far the coverage results carry over. The TE refers to the linked means and SDs, and individual scores add their own measurement error (Wu, 2005). With the delta method (Eq. 9), the TE carries over to derived reporting parameters such as proficiency level shares, for which LEs are rarely reported (Robitzsch & Lüdtke, 2024).

Recommendations for Practice

Under the assumptions of the M-estimation framework, the results suggest reporting the trend with the LE bc of the JK, the SE, and TE bc . These assumptions include IPD effects that are independent across items and participation that does not depend on the abilities. The JK recomputes the complete linking for every deleted item and thereby captures the item-selection variability of the estimator without the asymptotic approximation of the sandwich estimators, which explains why its intervals reached acceptable coverage at small numbers of items and under heavy-tailed IPD. Its costs are the 𝐼 recomputations per linking and a person-sampling bias correction that requires the full sampling covariance matrix of the calibrated item parameters LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS (Eq. S1), which the stacked calibration or the person bootstrap provides for dependent person samples. Because the sandwich-based intervals undercovered at 𝐼 = 15 and under PHL in part also at 𝐼 = 30, designs with at least 30 common items appear advisable when the sandwich estimators are used, in line with the general advice to raise the number of common items in LSAs (Mazzeo & von Davier, 2008; Weeks et al., 2014). Under heavy-tailed IPD, a small LE estimate does not rule out substantial IPD. The closed forms remain useful at the design stage, because they show how the common-item counts 𝐼 12 , 𝐼 23 , and 𝐼 123 and the IPD variances determine the LE before data are collected. Reporting both MGM and PHL, as in the empirical example, makes the sensitivity of the trend and its LE to the IPD process visible and treats the choice of the linking method as a further source of uncertainty, the model uncertainty (Longford, 2012).

Closed Forms Under General Zero-Mean IPD Processes

The closed-form LEs evaluate the estimating functions at the true parameter with infinite person samples. There, the identities (Eq. 2) reduce every component to a difference of true item parameters between two administrations on the T1 scale, up to known constants such as σ -1 2 in the second link of the chain. Under administration-specific effects that do not accumulate, every administration of an item adds an independent zero-mean effect to an item-specific level, and the IPD effects 𝑓 𝑖𝑡 and 𝑒 𝑖𝑡 are the differences of the administration-specific effects of consecutive administrations. With equal variances of the administration-specific effects across administrations, the IPD variances are equal across links,

The IPD effects of consecutive links share one administration-specific effect with opposite signs, which gives the cross-link covariances

Sandwich Matrices of MGM

At the true parameter, the MGM estimating function reduces to the population form given in the article after Equation ( 19). The discrimination IPD effects need no factor σ -1 2 , because a scale factor only adds a constant to differences of log item discriminations, which is absorbed by the log SD parameter.

Inserted into Equation (8), these entries give the meat matrix whose cross-link entries are multiplied by 𝐼 123 and vanish if 𝐶 1:3 is empty.

The bread matrix is

Its two subdiagonal entries, the expected derivatives of the mean equations with respect to the log SD parameters, are proportional to the differences µ 2 -b12 and µ 3 -b23 of the links, with the factor σ -1 2 reflecting the T2 scale of the second link. Through them, the uncertainty of the log SD estimates propagates to the mean estimates. With the gradients u σ = (σ 3 , 0, σ 3 , 0) ⊤ of σ3 = exp (s 2 + s 2,3 ) and u µ = (σ 2 µ 2,3 , 1, 0, σ 2 ) ⊤ of µ3 = µ 2 + σ 2 µ 2,3 , the delta method (Eq. 9) applied to the resulting sandwich variance yields the LEs of the linked T3 SD and mean in Equations ( 21) and ( 22) of the article.

Error Weights and Linking Error of the PHL Mean

For the linked T3 mean under PHL, the linearization (Eq. 6) with the error weights λ 𝑖 of Equation ( 25) gives with e 𝑖 = (𝑒 𝑖2 , 𝑒 𝑖3 ) ⊤ and the error-weighted mean item difficulties bλ2 = ∑︁ 𝑖 λ 𝑖2 𝑏 𝑖 and bλ3 = ∑︁ 𝑖 λ 𝑖3 𝑏 𝑖 .

For MGM, bλ2 = b12 and bλ3 = b23 , and the same decomposition reproduces Equation (20) of the article. The estimation error of the linked T2 log SD under PHL is ˆ︁ s 2s2 ≈ ∑︁ 𝑖 ν ⊤ 𝑖 f 𝑖 with the error weights

The error weights of 𝑓 𝑖2 sum to one and those of 𝑓 𝑖3 sum to zero, so that ˆ︁ s 2 does not respond to a shift of all discrimination IPD effects of the second link by the same amount. The items of 𝐶 2:3 receive a negative weight, because the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3 ties ˆ︁ s 3 to T1, so that part of a T2 ↔ T3 IPD effect is absorbed by ˆ︁ s 2 . Inserted into Equation (S21), these weights give

Because the error weights are constant within each common-item set up to the factor ω 𝑖 /𝑐, the LE of the linked T3 mean decomposes into the contributions of 𝐶 1:3 , 𝐶 1:2 , and 𝐶 2:3 as in Equation ( 27) of the article, with the coefficients

Under uniform IPD, all terms with ξ drop out, and the expression has the form of Equation ( 26) with σ3 = 1 and the difficulty IPD effects in place of the discrimination IPD effects.

In the limiting case with 𝐼123 = 0, the offsets reduce to κ 2 + κ3 = Δ 12 and κ3 = Δ 23 , and the first two terms reproduce the link contributions of Equation ( 22).

Limiting Cases for Three Time Points

If no item is administered at all three time points, so that 𝐼123 = 0, the cross-link terms of Equations ( 21) and ( 22) vanish, and the LEs of MGM chain linking become with the offsets Δ12 = µ 3 -b12 and Δ23 = µ 3 -b23 .

If every common item is administered at all three time points, so that 𝐼12 = 𝐼23 = 𝐼123 = 𝐼, Equations ( 21) and ( 22) become and with b = 𝐼 -1 ∑︁ 𝑖 𝑏 𝑖 and Δ12 = Δ23 = µ 3 -b.

Agreement of MGM and PHL in the Limiting Cases

If no item is administered at all three time points, the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3 of PHL is empty. The equation for s 3 then contains only the T2 ↔ T3 differences and yields the second-link solution for s 3s 2 . Inserting this solution into the equation for s 2 cancels the T2 ↔ T3 terms, and the first-link solution remains. The same argument applies to the mean equations, so the PHL estimates equal the estimates of chain linking (Engels et al., 2025). Because all items share 𝑚 𝑖 = 2, the item weights ω 𝑖 = 𝐼/2 are equal and cancel, and the estimates agree with unit weights as with ω 𝑖 = 𝐼/𝑚 𝑖.

If every common item is administered at all three time points, all three time-point pairs contribute to PHL, and the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3 compares the sums 𝑓 𝑖2 + 𝑓 𝑖3 and 𝑒 𝑖2 + 𝑒 𝑖3 of the IPD effects of both links. All items share the item weight ω 𝑖 = 𝐼/3, so the weighting leaves the estimates unchanged. Because every time-point pair is computed over the same complete item set, the pairwise condition of any two time points follows by adding the conditions of the links between them. The chain solution therefore satisfies the first-order conditions of the PHL criteria in Equation ( 23), and PHL reproduces the MGM estimates for both links.

In both designs, the two methods therefore define the same estimator, so they share the same LE and the same JK estimate. The sandwich estimators coincide as well. Under the reparameterization s3 = s 2 + s 2,3 and µ3 = µ 2 + σ 2 µ 2,3 , the PHL estimating function of each item is a linear transformation of its MGM estimating function, with a matrix that depends only on δ and is the same for all items. Because the estimating functions sum to zero at the estimate, the bread matrix, the meat matrix, and the sampling meat matrices transform accordingly, and the PHL sandwich variances equal the delta-method transforms of the MGM sandwich variances. The SE, LE bc , and the TE therefore agree as well.

Linking Error of MGM for Two Time Points

For two time points and 𝐼 common items, the parameter vector is δ = (s 2 , µ 2 ) ⊤ . With a single pair, every common item has the item weight ω 𝑖 = 𝐼/2, which cancels, and the first-order conditions of the PHL criteria are the MGM estimating equations, so PHL coincides with MGM (Engels et al., 2025). The LEs of the linked SD and of the linked mean, which therefore apply to both methods, are (Robitzsch, 2023) LE and with b = 𝐼 -1 ∑︁ 𝑖 𝑏 𝑖.

Simulation Study

The T2 results show the same qualitative pattern as the T3 results reported in the article. The intervals based on the SE undercovered in nearly all cells with IPD. For the linked mean, the TE-based intervals reached acceptable coverage in most cells, and for the linked SD, they overcovered more often, in line with the smaller true LEs of the SD parameters. The intervals based on the TE bc of the JK stayed within the acceptable range in nearly all cells for both parameters and both linking methods, whereas those based on the TE bc of the sandwich estimators fell below the acceptable range more often. The differences between MGM and PHL were smaller for the T2 parameters than for the T3 parameters.

Tables S2 to S9 and S12 to S16 report the remaining T3 results and the T2 results in the formats of Tables 1, 2, and 3 of the article.

A variance decomposition of the binary indicator of unacceptable coverage (Table S17) is consistent with the role of the IPD condition and the bias correction. The interaction of the IPD condition with the bias correction accounted for the largest share (22% and 25% for ˆ︁ µ 3 and ˆ︁ σ 3 ).

Further shares fell to the IPD condition (13% and 12%), the number of items (8% and 5%), and, for ˆ︁ σ 3 , the bias correction (15%), whereas the sample size, the LE estimator, and the linking method each accounted for at most 1%. The largest three-way terms were the interactions of the IPD condition with the number of items and the bias correction (3.4% and 2.2% for ˆ︁ µ 3 and ˆ︁ σ 3 ), with the number of items and the sample size (2.0% and 1.1%), with the sample size and the bias correction (1.7% and 1.6%), and, for ˆ︁ σ 3 , with the sample size and the LE estimator (1.5%). No other three-way term exceeded 1.5%, so the three-way structure mainly refines the dominant interaction of the IPD condition with the bias correction.

For a target quantity ℎ(δ), the LE and the SE combine as TE = √︁ SE 2 + LE 2 , with the LE of any of the estimators, and the bias-corrected TE is TE bc = √︃ SE 2 + LE 2 bc . Dependent Person Samples The separate calibrations estimate the sampling covariance matrix V ˆ︁ γ of the calibrated item parameters without sampling covariances between time points, which is correct under independent person samples. In many longitudinal designs, the same persons are assessed repeatedly, and the samples overlap only partially, because persons drop out, enter the study later, or are absent at individual time points. With the participation indicator 𝑧 𝑛𝑡 = 1 if person 𝑛 is assessed at time point 𝑡 and 𝑧 𝑛𝑡 = 0 otherwise, the union sample collects the 𝑁 ∪ = ∑︁ 𝑛 max 𝑡 𝑧 𝑛𝑡 persons assessed at least once, and 𝑁 𝑡 = ∑︁ 𝑛 𝑧 𝑛𝑡 of them are assessed at time point 𝑡. The 𝑁 𝑡𝑡 ′ = ∑︁ 𝑛 𝑧 𝑛𝑡 𝑧 𝑛𝑡 ′ persons assessed at both 𝑡 and 𝑡 ′ ≠ 𝑡, referred to as shared persons, make the cross-time-point blocks of V ˆ︁ γ nonzero. Only the estimate of V ˆ︁ γ changes, so the SE, LE bc , and the TE (Eqs. 11 to 15) are computed with the same formulas, whereas the LE estimates without bias correction do not depend on V ˆ︁ γ at all.

PHL additionally uses the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3, which skips T2 and is therefore not a link. For the T1 ↔ T2 link of MGM, log ˆ︁ 𝑎 𝑖2 -log ˆ︁ 𝑎 𝑖1 -s2 = log 𝑎 𝑖2 -log 𝑎 𝑖1 and exp (s 2 ) ˆ︁ 𝑏 𝑖2 -ˆ︁ 𝑏 𝑖1 +µ2 = 𝑏 𝑖2 -𝑏 𝑖1 , and the difference in the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3 of PHL telescopes into the sum of the differences in the two links, for example, 𝑏 𝑖3 -𝑏 𝑖1 = (𝑏 𝑖2 -𝑏 𝑖1 ) + (𝑏 𝑖3 -𝑏 𝑖2 ). These reductions use only the identities and the differencing, not the IPD process. For any IPD process, the IPD effects of Equation (3) are therefore the changes of the item parameters between consecutive time points on the T1 scale, 𝑓 𝑖𝑡 = log 𝑎 𝑖𝑡log 𝑎 𝑖,𝑡-1 and 𝑒 𝑖𝑡 = 𝑏 𝑖𝑡 -𝑏 𝑖,𝑡-1(S8)and the error representations of the article (Eqs. 20 and 25) hold without change, because the error weights depend only on the common-item counts, the item weights, and fixed true parameters. If the IPD effects have zero means, are independent across items, and have finite second moments, the closed-form LEs are the standard deviations of these fixed linear combinations, with the variances and covariances of the IPD effects inserted in 𝚽. The zero means remain the identifying assumption, and the random walk is the special case in which the IPD effects of different links are uncorrelated.

Note. Bias = mean of the linked estimates across the 4000 replications minus the linked parameter. Dist = IPD distribution (N = normal, 𝑡3 = scaled 𝑡 with three degrees of freedom). IPD = IPD level (Weak: τ 𝑒 = 0.25, τ 𝑓 = 0.125; Strong: τ 𝑒 = 0.5, τ 𝑓 = 0.25).

Inf = bias with infinite person samples. MGM = mean-geometric mean linking; PHL = pairwise Haberman linking. Bold: absolute bias larger than 0.01, based on unrounded values.

Note. Coverage of nominal 95% confidence intervals; 4000 replications. Dist = IPD distribution (N = normal, 𝑡3 = scaled 𝑡 with three degrees of freedom). IPD = IPD level (Weak: τ 𝑒 = 0.25, τ 𝑓 = 0.125; Strong: τ 𝑒 = 0.5, τ 𝑓 = 0.25). TE combines the SE with the linking error (LE) of the column estimator; TE bc uses its bias-corrected LE. Inf = coverage with infinite person samples, where the TE equals the LE. JK = jackknife; ESW = expected sandwich; BOSW = bias-corrected observed sandwich. MGM = mean-geometric mean linking; PHL = pairwise Haberman linking. Bold: outside [92.5, 97.5].
